text: Last lesson drew a line around the Kubernetes workload itself and called that the portable core. But a workload doesn't exist in isolation — it talks to a message queue, it talks to a database, and the moment its code calls a cloud SDK directly, all the portability you just built upstream stops mattering, because the coupling isn't about where the container runs anymore. It's about what the container's own code is written against.

The fix is a pattern you'd reach for in any well-factored application: define the capability as an interface, and push every cloud-specific detail into an adapter behind it. A MessageQueue interface exposes exactly three methods — send, receive, ack — and nothing in your business logic ever imports azure.servicebus or boto3. It just calls queue.send on whatever object it was handed.

Behind that interface sit two concrete adapters. AzureServiceBusQueue implements it using the real Service Bus SDK. SqsQueue implements the identical interface using boto3 against SQS. Neither adapter knows about the other, and application code never imports either one directly — it only ever sees the MessageQueue type. The exact same discipline applies to a database: an OrderRepository interface with get, save, and list methods lets Azure SQL Database and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL sit behind the same calling code, as long as the schema itself is genuinely portable SQL.

So where does the actual cloud decision get made? In exactly one place — a factory function that reads a CLOUD_PROVIDER environment variable and returns the right adapter. Everywhere else in the codebase only ever depends on the interface. That's what makes this different from scattering if-Azure-else-AWS branches through business logic: the decision is centralized, and it's the only part of the system that has to change when you add a third cloud or drop one.

None of this is free, and it's worth saying so plainly. An interface built to satisfy two providers narrows to their common ground — Service Bus sessions and SQS FIFO deduplication can't both be fully exposed without the interface becoming leaky. It's a second test suite and a second set of provider failure modes to maintain, forever. And it only pays for itself when you'll genuinely run more than one implementation — building this for a workload that will only ever run on Azure is pure overhead. Next lesson takes the same instinct into Terraform itself, provisioning across clouds from one configuration.
